name: Nimoa
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: p.463: "I have heard reports which suggest that there is phonemic stress in this language." p.475: "I mention length first, to distinguish length from stress. Stress is phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima, and probably also in Nimowa and Sud-Est. Stress is not indicated in any practical orthography. In all of the languages of PTC it seems that stress is predictable within certain word-classes, notably kinship nouns and verbs. When a kinship noun is pluralised by the addition of a suffix, the stress moves one syllable closer to the end of the word."
new_statements.citation: Lithgow, David R. 1976. Austronesian languages: Milne Bay and adjacent islands (Milne Bay Province). In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages (Pacific Linguistics C-39), 441-523. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C39.441.
new_statements.locator: p.463, sec. 59 NIMOWA (last sentence); p.475, sec. 84 STRESS (first paragraph)
new_statements.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only published statement says stress is probably phonemic (contrastive) in Nimowa, on the strength of reports Lithgow had heard, with a cluster-wide observation that stress is predictable inside kinship nouns and verbs and shifts one syllable rightward when a suffix is added. No placement rule is given for Nimowa. The Henderson & Henderson 1974 wordlist as re-typed in ABVD marks stress on the penultimate syllable in nearly every polysyllable (closed final syllables and reduplicants excepted), which points to a penultimate default, but that is data I read second-hand, not a description.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Nimowa; the cluster-wide note says stress moves rightward under plural and object suffixation.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (Lithgow's sec. 84 is framed around 'the phonological word'); statement is hedged ('reports which suggest', 'probably') and gives no position.
new_statements.identity_note: Nimoa = Nimowa = Rifao [nmw], glottocode nimo1246. Lithgow 1976 p.452 defines the language as Western Point on Sud-Est plus the islands Nimowa, Panatinani, Sabari and Panawina, with widely divergent dialects (cognate 75-92%); the 2014 ISO request renames it Rifao with dialects Nimowa, Saisai, Sabal. MacGillivray's 1852 'Brierly Island' vocabulary (11°20'S 153°9'E) and Ray 1937's Panatinani data fall inside this area. Lithgow's statements name 'Nimowa' as the whole language, not a single dialect. Sudest [tgo, sude1239] is the sister language; its penultimate-with-schwa-retraction stress (Sheppard 2020, SIL OPD) is not evidence for Nimoa.

sources.note: Survey chapter with a short section on Nimowa (sec. 59, p.463) and a general sec. 84 STRESS (p.475). p.463: 'I have heard reports which suggest that there is phonemic stress in this language.' p.475: 'Stress is phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima, and probably also in Nimowa and Sud-Est. Stress is not indicated in any practical orthography.' Then a cluster-wide remark that stress is predictable within certain word classes (kinship nouns, verbs) and moves one syllable rightward when a plural or object suffix is added. No placement rule for Nimowa. Both passages verified on page images…

sources.citation: Henderson, Jim & Anne Henderson. 1974. Languages of the Louisiade Archipelago and environs. Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 3 (Three studies in languages of eastern Papua, ed. Alan Healey), 39-61. Ukarumpa: SIL. -- as re-typed in ABVD language 669 'Nimoa' (typed by Ger Reesink, checked by Simon Greenhill).
sources.note: Only the 83-item wordlist reached me, second-hand via ABVD (https://abvd.eva.mpg.de/austronesian/language.php?id=669; HTML saved). 46 forms carry a stress mark; the mark sits on the penultimate syllable in nearly all of them (ni'mʌnɛ 'hand', hɛ'hɛnɛ 'leg', mʌ'tʌnɛ 'eye', bu'sunɛ 'nose', ŋi'ŋinɛ 'tooth', la'hinɛ 'big', ṱa'lɛyʌn 'star', i'wuwo 'fly'), on a closed final syllable in two (hɛ'dʌm 'name', řʌ'kikʔŋ 'cold'), and on both halves of reduplications (yalu'yalu, bwʌhi'bwʌhi). This is data, not a statement; the original paper (SIL-PNG record 23648, 'Not Available Online') was not reached.

sources.citation: MacGillivray, John. 1852. Narrative of the voyage of H.M.S. Brierly Island, lat. 11°20'S, long. 153°9'E, plus Duchateau Isles words from Calvados Group natives), pp. 317ff. London: Boone.
sources.note: Brierly Island coordinates match the Nimoa point (Ray 1907 treats this list as Louisiade data; 'bushuda' nose matches ABVD Nimoa bu'sunɛ). Bare wordlist; no accent marks, no remarks on accent or emphasis.
